children: Indian banks are well-positioned to absorb potential mark-to-market treasury hits in the July-September quarter of 2026 (Q2FY27), driven by robust credit growth of 17% to 18%, according to Digant Haria, founder of GreenEdge Wealth Services.

Assessing the second-quarter business updates, Haria highlighted standout performances across the financial sector. He noted strong deposit growth for HDFC Bank and praised non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) such as Bajaj Finance and L&T Finance, alongside small finance banks like Equitas Small Finance Bank and Ujjivan Small Finance Bank. Public sector lenders, particularly Bank of India and Union Bank of India, are "flying around with 17-18% growth," a level he noted has not been seen in a while.

Addressing concerns over net interest margin (NIM) compression, Haria expects the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to implement a token rate hike of 25 to 50 basis points on October 7 in response to rising global bond yields. "We don't need that as such if we just look at India, but because the global bond deals are moving the way, I think RBI will have to do some 25-50 bps, you know, a token to show that, you know, if needed, we are ready to take that price hike or the rate hike," he said.

This potential move should benefit the banking sector, as more than 50% of bank portfolios are linked to the external benchmark lending rate (EBLR). While NBFCs might face margin pressures depending on the central bank's tone, Haria remains bullish on banks, noting that the only hurdle is foreign institutional investor (FII) selling and general market sentiment.

Responding to queries about rising Indian 10-year yields impacting treasury books, Haria emphasized that the current growth trajectory provides a strong cushion. "The 12-13% growth versus a 16-17% growth is a world of a difference because you have so much more money and so much more operating leverage that can kick in your P&Ls," he explained.

Margins likely hit rock bottom in the previous quarter for lenders like Axis Bank, paving the way for stabilisation or slight improvement. Haria concluded that there is nothing negative visible for the September quarter, with the RBI's upcoming policy decision set to define the trajectory for the next few quarters.
